description: An interactive study map for MAT 412. Test 1 follows Howell & Mathews through §3.2 (handout 2.1–2.5 and 3.1–3.2). Test 2 is §4.1 and §4.2.
throughline: One point has two addresses. Cartesian says where it sits; polar says how to reach it. A function is a motion, and a derivative is that motion seen up close. Every stop asks you to watch one motion and name the address that makes it obvious.
footer: A study map for MAT 412, citing Howell & Mathews, Complex Analysis (CC BY 4.0), at about 90% confidence. It runs in your browser and works offline.

threads.title: One point, two addresses
threads.summary: Cartesian says where z sits. Polar says how to reach it. Pick the native address.

threads.title: The staircase: z, arg z, Arg z
threads.summary: A move has infinitely many names. arg z is all of them. Arg z is the home step.

threads.title: A function is a motion
threads.summary: A differentiable map, seen up close, is one spin and one stretch. No mirror.

threads.title: One rule, every starting point
threads.summary: The colour of a point is what the rule does if you start there.

test1.text: Blue is the Cartesian address: where z sits. Across by x, up by y.
Orange is the polar address: how to reach z. Turn by θ, stretch by r.
Green is the point you drag.
Purple is where a function sends that point.

test2.text: Blue is a walk that stayed, or the blue Newton root.
Orange is a walk that escaped, or the orange Newton root. On Julia it is also the handle c.
Purple is the third Newton root.
Green is the point you drag: one walk, or one guess.

stations.title: The Map
stations.summary: The story of the course on one map.
stations.observe: Drag the one point, then use the finder or the map. The dot is the only control on that picture.

viz.sentence: One point. Blue drops say where it sits. The orange ray says how to reach it.

source.note: The map covers the handout through 3.2, which lines up with Howell & Mathews 2.1–2.5 and 3.1–3.2. Chapter 1 titles are the handout's.

stations.title: One Point, Two Addresses
stations.summary: Drag one point. Its Cartesian address and its polar address update together.
stations.observe: Watch the blue drops and the orange ray name the same dot. Arg jumps on the negative real axis. The dot does not.

source.note: Handout section title. Howell & Mathews Chapter 1 uses different section titles.

viz.sentence: Cartesian says where it sits. Polar says how to reach it. They are the same point.

stations.title: Slide, Spin, Stretch, Mirror
stations.summary: Adding slides. Multiplying spins and stretches. Conjugation mirrors.
stations.observe: Watch two arrows. Addition is a slide. Multiplication turns and stretches. The mirror flips the height.

source.note: Handout section title. Howell & Mathews Chapter 1 uses different section titles.

stations.title: Length, Distance, Circles
stations.summary: |z| is a ray length. |z1 − z2| is a slide length. |z − a| = R is a circle.
stations.observe: Read |z − a| = R as a sentence about distance before you square anything.

source.note: Handout section title. Howell & Mathews Chapter 1 uses different section titles.

stations.title: The Staircase: z, arg z, Arg z
stations.summary: The angle you walk is smooth. Arg, the name of that angle, jumps at π.
stations.observe: Drag x across π. The purple value is Arg. It jumps. The x you dragged does not.

claim.whenTrue: Arg is still positive. You have not crossed π, so the name and the walk agree.
claim.whenFalse: Arg is negative. You crossed π. The walk kept going. The name jumped.

source.note: Handout §1.3, not a Howell & Mathews section number. The book defines Arg in §1.4 The Geometry of Complex Numbers, Part II (Definition 1.4.6): the value in (−π, π]. This graph is that wrap.

stations.title: Powers: Spin n Times
stations.summary: z, z², …, zⁿ as a spiral. The polar column does the work.
stations.observe: Each extra power turns the same angle again and multiplies the length.

source.note: Handout section title. Howell & Mathews Chapter 1 uses different section titles.

stations.title: Roots: Divide the Staircase
stations.summary: Divide the full turn by n. You land on n equally spaced points.
stations.observe: Count the gaps. Five gaps means the fifth roots of 1. Four or six does not.

claim.whenTrue: Five equal gaps on the circle. These are the fifth roots of 1.
claim.whenFalse: The gaps are equal, and there are not five of them. These are not the fifth roots of 1.

source.note: Handout §1.4 and exercise 1.4.1. Howell & Mathews puts the nth roots of unity in §1.5 The Algebra of Complex Numbers, Part II, equation (1.5.5): equally spaced on the unit circle. The book's §1.4 is polar geometry.

stations.title: Curves and Time
stations.summary: A curve z(t) is a point moving on one clock.
stations.observe: Scrub time. The point moves. The clock, not the shape, is the definition.

source.sectionTitle: Sets of Points in the Complex Plane
source.note: Handout section title. Howell & Mathews Chapter 1 uses different section titles.

stations.title: Disks, Annuli, Boundaries
stations.summary: Open, closed, bounded, connected: each is a sentence about a tiny disk.
stations.observe: Park a tiny disk on a point. The set is open there when the disk fits inside.

source.sectionTitle: Sets of Points in the Complex Plane
source.note: Handout section title. Howell & Mathews Chapter 1 uses different section titles.

stations.title: A Function Is a Motion
stations.summary: Multiplication by i is a quarter turn of the square. The exercise writes z² + iz; this picture is the turn the hint names.
stations.observe: Drag the angle. At a quarter turn the square has been multiplied by i. At a half turn it has not.

claim.whenTrue: A quarter turn. This is multiplication by i. The square is still a square.
claim.whenFalse: This turn is not multiplication by i.

source.note: Handout prompt, not a book exercise. In Howell & Mathews, (2.1.1) is the equation f = u + iv. Section exercises are numbered 1, 2, 3. Example 2.1.6 writes z² as u+iv. Example 2.1.11 is multiplication by i, the turn this picture shows.

stations.title: Linear Maps: Spin, Stretch, Slide
stations.summary: az + b is a turn, a stretch, and a slide, in that order.
stations.observe: Change a and only the turn-and-stretch changes. Change b and the picture slides.

stations.title: z^n: Fans and Parabolas
stations.summary: A polar grid survives zⁿ. A Cartesian grid bends.
stations.observe: Send a ray and a circle through z². They stay a ray and a circle. A vertical line does not.

source.sectionTitle: The Mappings w = z^n and w = z^(1/n)

stations.title: Principal Roots: Stand on the Home Step
stations.summary: The n roots sit on a circle. The principal root is the one on the home step.
stations.observe: Sweep the input around 0. The principal root jumps when the input crosses the seam.

source.sectionTitle: The Mappings w = z^n and w = z^(1/n)

stations.title: Branches and Cuts
stations.summary: A branch is a choice of angle. The cut is where that choice jumps.
stations.observe: Walk across the cut. The value jumps. Walk the long way around and it does not.

stations.title: 1/z and the Sphere
stations.summary: 1/z inverts the length and mirrors. Infinity becomes a place on the sphere.
stations.observe: Watch the circle through 0 open into a line. That line is the picture of inversion.

stations.title: Limits: Every Direction Must Agree
stations.summary: A limit exists only when every path into the point agrees.
stations.observe: Approach 0 along two paths. If the values disagree, there is no limit. One path is never enough.

stations.title: The Derivative Is a Move
stations.summary: Up close, a derivative is one spin and one stretch. A shear is a smear, not a derivative.
stations.observe: Drag from the turn to the shear. The image stays a square only while the motion is a spin and a stretch.

claim.whenTrue: The image is a square: one spin and one stretch. That is what a derivative looks like.
claim.whenFalse: The image is a smear. A derivative does not do this.

source.note: §3.1 defines the derivative as the limit of Δw/Δz (equation 3.1.1). That limit is multiplication by one complex number: a turn and a stretch. A shear is not that limit. This stop has no numbered exercise.

stations.title: Cauchy-Riemann: No Mirror
stations.summary: The two real derivatives must describe one turn-and-stretch, not a flip.
stations.observe: Check u_x against v_y and u_y against −v_x. A mirror fails that pair.

stations.title: The Mapping Lab
stations.summary: Draw on the z-plane and watch it move under f.
stations.observe: Draw a guess of the image, then let the map move. The surprise is the lesson.

stations.title: The 4D Graph
stations.summary: The graph of w = f(z) needs four dimensions. A picture is a shadow of it.
stations.observe: Name which shadow you are looking at: real part, imaginary part, modulus, or the Riemann surface.

stations.title: Flashcards
stations.summary: Say the back out loud, then show it.
stations.observe: If you cannot say the back, go to the stop named on the card and watch the picture.

stations.summary: Read the question, take the hint, then open the answer.
stations.observe: Name the stop and the address before you open the answer.

source.note: Each card cites its own exercise. Chapter 1 titles follow the handout; Howell & Mathews numbers that chapter differently.

stations.title: Julia Sets: Square, then Slide
stations.summary: The rule is square, then slide by c. The solid region is every start whose walk stays near 0.
stations.observe: Leave c at 0 and see a disk. Drag c until the disk breaks. Blue stayed. The orange handle is c.

source.note: Filled Julia set K_c is §4.2. The orbit of a start is also §4.1 Sequences and Series.

stations.title: Newton Fractals: Which Root?
stations.summary: The colour of a starting point is which root Newton's method finds from there.
stations.observe: Open on z³ − 1. Drag a root and watch its colour follow. Green is one guess.

source.note: Newton's method and the basins of the roots are §4.2.

flashcards.front: What do the two addresses of one point say?
flashcards.back: Cartesian says where it sits (x, y). Polar says how to reach it (turn, then stretch).

source.note: Handout section title. Howell & Mathews Chapter 1 uses different section titles.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between arg z and Arg z?
flashcards.back: arg z is every angle that lands on z. Arg z is the one name in (−π, π].

source.note: Handout §1.3. The book defines arg z as the set of angles and Arg z as the one in (−π, π], in §1.4 Definition 1.4.4 and Definition 1.4.6.

flashcards.front: What does multiplication do to the polar address?
flashcards.back: Lengths multiply. Names of the angle add.

source.note: Handout section title. Howell & Mathews Chapter 1 uses different section titles.

flashcards.front: Why are there n n-th roots?
flashcards.back: The staircase of angles has a step every full turn. Dividing by n hits n distinct steps before it repeats.

source.note: Handout exercise 1.4.1. The book states the nth roots of unity in §1.5, equation (1.5.5), not as exercise 1.4.1.

flashcards.front: What is a complex function, as a picture?
flashcards.back: A motion: each point of the z-plane is sent to a point of the w-plane.
When two paths into the point produce two different values. Every path has to agree.

flashcards.front: What do the Cauchy-Riemann equations forbid?
flashcards.back: A mirror. Up close the map must be one spin and one stretch: u_x = v_y and u_y = −v_x.

flashcards.front: What is the filled Julia set of z² + c?
flashcards.back: Every starting point whose walk, square then slide by c, stays near 0.

source.note: Filled Julia set K_c is §4.2. The orbit of a start is also §4.1 Sequences and Series.

problems.statement: Let $z_1 = 3 - 2i$ and $z_2 = -1 + 4i$. Compute $z_1 z_2$ and $z_1/z_2$ in the form $x + iy$.
problems.hint: Multiply by the definition. For the quotient, multiply top and bottom by the mirror of $z_2$.

source.note: Handout exercise number. Answer worked here. Howell & Mathews Chapter 1 uses different section titles.

problems.statement: Sketch the set of points that satisfy $|z - (1 + 2i)| = 3$.
problems.hint: Read the sentence as a distance. Do not expand it yet.

answer.tex: The circle with centre $1+2i$ and radius $3$.

source.note: Handout exercise number. Answer worked here. Howell & Mathews Chapter 1 uses different section titles.

problems.statement: Write $z = -1 + i\sqrt{3}$ in polar form and exponential form. What is $\operatorname{Arg}(z)$?
problems.hint: The dot is already on the picture. Read the length and the home-step angle.

source.note: Handout exercise number. Answer worked here. Howell & Mathews Chapter 1 uses different section titles.

problems.statement: Find and sketch the 5th roots of unity.
problems.hint: Divide the staircase of $1$ by $5$. The points are equally spaced on the unit circle.

source.note: Handout exercise 1.4.1, the fifth roots of unity. Howell & Mathews states them in §1.5, equation (1.5.5). The book's §1.4 is polar geometry. Answer worked here.

problems.statement: Express $f(z) = z^2 + iz$ as $u + iv$ in both addresses.
problems.hint: Expand $x+iy$, and also write the polar form. Multiplication by $i$ is a quarter turn.

answer.tex: $u = x^2 - y^2 - y$, $v = 2xy + x$. In polar, $r^2 e^{i 2\theta} + r e^{i(\theta+\pi/2)}$.
answer.text: u = x^2 - y^2 - y, v = 2xy + x

source.note: Handout prompt, not a book exercise. (2.1.1) in the book is the equation f = u + iv. Section exercises are numbered 1, 2, 3. Answer worked here.

problems.statement: For $f(z) = e^x(\cos y + i\sin y)$, use the Cauchy-Riemann equations to show $f$ is entire, and compute $f'(z)$.
problems.hint: Write $u$ and $v$. Compare $u_x$ with $v_y$ and $u_y$ with $-v_x$.

answer.tex: The equations hold everywhere and the partials are continuous, so $f$ is entire and $f' = f$.
answer.text: f is entire and f' = f
